speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON MEETING OP CANADA-JAPAN MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to report on the recent meeting of the Canada-Japan ministerial committee from which my colleagues and I returned last evening, and to table the final communique of the meeting.
The establishment of this ministerial committee was agreed upon in 1961 at the time of Prime Minister Ikeda's visit to Ottawa. This third meeting took place in the foreign ministry in Tokyo on September 4 and 5.
Japan was represented by the ministers of foreign affairs, finance, agriculture and forestry, and international trade and industry; by the director of the economic planning agency, and by Mr. Hisanaga Shimazu, the new ambassador to Canada. The ministers of finance, trade and commerce, fisheries, myself and the Canadian ambassador to Japan, Mr. Bower, formed the Canadian delegation.
Tnis was a useful meeting. We made progress, I believe, in mutual understanding. The ministerial committee is not a negotiating body. It provides a forum in which ministers from the two countries can exchange views on relations between Canada and Japan and on international problems. We now understand better the Japanese point of view on many questions, and I think they better understand ours.
We found that Canada and Japan have to almost all situations a common approach based on common beliefs in freedom, justice and the desirability of measures to promote world prosperity. We noted the numerous occasions on which our delegations have worked together at the United Nations, particularly in the promotion of the treaty to
suspend nuclear testing. Japan shares with Canada the belief that the United Nations remains the main hope for the promotion of peace in the world, and the determination that the organization should be strengthened and its finances assured. We engaged as well in discussions on the role of the United Nations in peace keeping operations.
The committee had an interesting exchange of views on the various political situations in Asia. The Japanese, like us, are concerned over the Indonesian conflict with Malaysia and share our hope that the dispute will be settled by peaceful means in accordance with the charter of the United Nations. The committee agreed as well on the urgent necessity of restoring stability and of improving the well being of the Vietnamese and the other Indochinese peoples. We found that, like ourselves, the Japanese were giving careful thought to the problem of communist China. In this and many other fields we are resolved to continue to work together in close consultation, convinced that Canada and Japan as neighbouring countries across the Pacific have a consequential role to play in the promotion of stability and in the economic development of the Asian and Pacific regions.
We reviewed the current economic position and prospects for the two economies. Canadian ministers were much impressed by the determination and purpose with which the government and people of Japan are pursuing their policies of modernization and economic growth. There is every reason to believe that Canadian expoits to Japan, which have risen so rapidly in recent years, will continue to expand at a good rate as a result both of expansion of the Japanese economy and further trade liberalization.
We discussed in some detail the various quantitative restrictions and other Japanese obstacles to trade which still limit sales of Canadian goods to Japan. We expressed our expectation of early progress in liberalizing remaining Japanese restrictions and of important and meaningful negotiations between Japan and Canada in the course of the current Kennedy round of trade and tariff negotiations.
The Japanese ministers drew attention to the imbalance of trade with Canada and to

Canada-Japan Ministerial Meeting the inhibition of their sales to Canada represented by the restraints they observe on exports of certain of their products to this country to avoid disruption of our market. Canadian ministers noted that nearly all Canadian exports to Japan are essential foodstuffs or necessary industrial material, which provide the sinews of Japanese economic strength. On the other hand, most Japanese exports are manufactures and directly competitive with Canadian production. In the circumstances a trade imbalance is not unnatural.
Both sides were agreed on the desirability of an expansion of trade in both directions. It was noted that there was a variety of opportunities for the further diversification of Japanese sales to Canada. In this regard a high level Japanese economic mission will be visiting Canada in October.
Our discussions led to an improved understanding of the problem of voluntary restraints as seen from the two sides. Canadian ministers noted in this regard that no other highly industrialized country extends more liberal treatment than does Canada to Japanese imports. The communique records our agreement that recourse to such restraints should be kept to a minimum and that necessary consultations in this regard should be expeditious and based on mutual understanding.
We had an excellent exchange of views about international economic matters, including the status of the Kennedy round, international liquidity, the trade and development problems of the less advanced countries and east-west trade. In all these important matters there was a remarkable and gratifying similarity of interest and outlook. We found ourselves in full agreement on the objectives of trade liberalization to be pursued through the Kennedy round and expressed determination to do our respective parts to make the negotiations a success. Ministers specifically agreed to maintain close co-operation between their respective delegations throughout these important negotiations.
There was useful discussion of fisheries matters. We considered the problems facing the meeting of the parties to the north Pacific convention which opens here in Ottawa tomorrow. As a result we are hopeful that a formula will be found which will adequately reflect the interests of the three countries and result in the maintenance and development of the vital fisheries resources of the north Pacific. Other fisheries questions


were considered, including the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act of Canada. I am satisfied that as an outcome of our discussions the extent of fisheries co-operation between Canada and Japan has been enlarged and will be intensified in the years to come.
We renewed our invitation to Japan to participate in Expo '67, and we trust that a decision will soon be taken to permit a worthy representation in Montreal of the traditional culture and modern accomplishments of our Pacific neighbour.
The Minister of Finance took advantage of his visit to Japan to sign on behalf of Canada an agreement for the avoidance of double taxation and the prevention of fiscal evasion with respect to taxes on income. This agreement will be submitted to the house and to the Japanese Diet for approval before ratification.
I signed on behalf of Canada an exchange of notes covering the mutual waiver of certain visa requirements between the two countries.
In a different field we noted the progress made in the development of communication satellites, an area which offers the prospect of extensive future co-operation between our two countries.
I would like to express my gratitude for the conversations I was privileged to have with the Japanese prime minister. Mr. Ikeda added his personal views on many subjects, and I was particularly impressed with his qualities of statesmanship and his understanding of the international scene.
I wish to mention the all too brief visit the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I were able to make to the city of Hiroshima. We were deeply moved. The indelible message of Hiroshima cannot be adequately expressed in words. It must never be forgotten, even though a fine new city all but covers the scars.
Japan, after the United States and Great Britain, is Canada's most important trading partner, and these ministerial meetings have provided a valuable opportunity for developing closer relations with this great Pacific nation as a neighbour and a friend.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REPORT ON MEETING OP CANADA-JAPAN MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the summary given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs regarding the ministerial meetings in Japan does reveal one continuing fact, namely the close relationship between the Japanese and the Canadian peoples. The minister mentioned the visit to Hiroshima, a visit that

could result only in a greater determination that never again shall there be resort to nuclear arms. It shows the utter devastation that results from the use of an instrument which, while a tremendous power for good, also represents the sword of potential destruction.
As to the references by the minister to the Prime Minister of Japan, may I say that anyone who has met with Mr. Ikeda cannot be other than greatly impressed not only by his knowledge of international affairs, to which the minister alluded, but as well by the wealth of friendship which he shows in everything he says and does in relation to Canada.
As to what took place, I think the house will be disappointed that it has not received some concrete information. Amidst a mass of generalities and grandiloquent prose, all that emerges is that these meetings are beneficial; and they are. But what action was determined upon is left to the imagination.
In our trading relations with Japan the imbalance of trade is a matter that has continued throughout the years. I do not forget that when we were in office the Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, on more than one occasion expressed his great concern respecting our trade imbalance with Japan. I recall one time in particular, on February 23, 1962, when he asked whether the Japanese authorities were "becoming embittered by the efforts of the federal government to keep a tight lid on exports from their country to Canada, despite a continuing increase in Canadian sales to Japan". The view of the Liberal party of that day, if that question meant what it apparently did, was that we should not endeavour, by securing mutual quotas, to prevent the dumping or the export to Canada of products in the production which Canadians could not compete. However, since the present government has come into office it has generally followed the course of the previous government despite the protestations to the contrary in the past.
Sir, all of us in this house recognize that Japan, who only a few short years ago was a major enemy, has in the intervening comparatively few years since the end of the war become an exponent of democracy, a country which practises democracy and whose watchwords are freedom and liberty, having a desire to walk side by side with the free nations in maintaining freedom in all parts of the world as well as at all times standing firmly against the onrush of communism.
Canada-Japan Ministerial Meeting Mr. T. C. Douglas (Burnaby-Coquillam):
Mr. Speaker, members in all parts of the house will welcome the return of the delegation of Canadian ministers from their visit to Tokyo, and we are glad to have the report today from the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I think it is encouraging to know that representatives of the Canadian government can sit down with the cabinet ministers of Japan, and that a nation with which a few years ago we were at war should now be willing to agree that the various international differences that affect the world must be worked out within the charter of the United Nations. I think we can now confidently hope that our days of difference with Japan are behind us, and that before us stretches a new vista of peaceful co-operation.
I was particularly impressed with the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs regarding the liberalization of trade between Canada and Japan. The minister spoke in most optimistic terms. However, this statement is hardly in accord with that made by the Minister of Finance according to a Tokyo report, which says:
Finance Minister Walter Gordon of Canada said yesterday his government will not tolerate damage to well established Canadian industries by unrestrained imports on low cost Japanese goods.
The minister went on to say:
This year these restraints apply mostly to textiles, footwear and tableware and make up only one quarter of Japan's total exports to Canada of $150 million.
Then the report goes on to say that no agreement was reached on the issue of Japanese worsteds, and it points out that the Japanese government are not satisfied that Canadian industry is being hurt by the import of Japanese worsteds into this country.
I think we must recognize, Mr. Speaker, that Japan offers a great market for Canada, particularly for western Canada, and it is very important to our future economic development. We must also recognize that Japan buys from us a great deal more than we buy from her, and that if this trade is to continue we must open up avenues by which Japan can sell her goods in Canada. This might have to be a gradual adjustment of present voluntary restrictions, but it must be definite and must not merely consist of platitudes. I hope before long we will have some definitive statement from the government as to how much this liberalization of trade is to be a reality and how much of it is to be a myth.
There is one other thing I should like to say, that the minister's statement with reference to Hiroshima I am sure impressed all of

Canada-Japan Ministerial Meeting us. I think it is not only important that we say it will never be forgotten; I think we must also resolve that it will never be repeated.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON MEETING OP CANADA-JAPAN MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we join in welcoming the Secretary of State for External Affairs and other members of the delegation who have returned from their journey to Japan. I believe we have a mutual feeling of appreciation for the abbreviated but still comprehensive report the minister has made to us in respect of the negotiations and actions taken in Japan at this ministerial conference.
It is significant that this particular conference should have taken place as it did, just prior to the Olympic games which will shortly begin in Japan. I think both serve to remind us of that ever-narrowing world which brings us all, nation and nation, citizen and citizen, closer together.
References to Hiroshima that have already been made, are something that strike close to the hearts of all peace-loving people and reminds us all of the awfulness of the age in which we live, should those scientific inventions that have been brought to reality be used for purposes other than peaceful development.
It is discouraging that in his remarks the minister had to mention the problem that exists today between our fellow commonwealth nations, Malaysia and Indonesia, and that the threat of war still hangs heavy in many parts of the world.
Obviously the bulk of the discussions that took place had to do with trade. The minister's remarks reminded us very clearly that trade is a two-way street, and that we cannot expect to sell unless we are likewise willing to buy. We in the west are particularly interested in the potential of trade with Japan. Within these few days while this conference has been taking place a group of Japanese industrialists have been investigating the potentials with respect to the coal necessary to feed the furnaces of Japan, in my own constituency. It is true that we have a tremendous potential in trade with Japan, but this will not come to pass unless the talks which have just taken place are extended so they become mutually satisfactory arrangements.
Certainly there is something most commendable in the fact that two countries such as Japan and Canada can sit down at the level which these talks took place and discuss these problems, and then arrive at voluntary

restraints upon each other's policies, in an effort to assist each other, as they at the same time seek to ease those burdens that each nation has relating to this problem of trade. It is noted also that the minister mentioned the fisheries problems, and we know these are urgent. We are pleased that this subject has been discussed as well.
It is not necessary to go into great detail at this time, Mr. Speaker, except to say again that I think it is encouraging to find negotiations of this type taking place at this level which can also bring about such courtesies and convenient arrangements regarding visas and taxation which are to the mutual advantage of the citizens of both nations.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, we welcome this report and look forward to more details of the discussions, and the opportunity for debate at a later date in the house.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON MEETING OP CANADA-JAPAN MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement just made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs was certainly most interesting. The members of this house and the Canadian people will readily appreciate that, besides being one of the largest markets for Canadian products, Japan can also supply us with items that are not produced here.
We export goods and industrial equipment to Japan and, in so doing, we find that in addition to assisting that country, we are also helping Canadian producers. The minister is convinced that Japan represents one of the best foreign outlets in the world for our export products.
One point on which I quite agree with the minister is this. I much prefer seeing him do business with Japan than with the communist countries of the world. I doubt that Japan will use Canadian products to try through economic means to win the world over to a communist ideology. The Japanese respect the human being, just as we do here in Canada, and I feel that we must do everything that is humanly possible to improve relations between our country and Japan.
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, I wish to repeat that ahead of the Japanese market or any other market throughout the world, there is a domestic market which is not satisfied and I am anxious to see the day when the members of the cabinet, led by the Prime Minister, will propose to us solutions or means to

satisfy the domestic market first, that is the Canadian consumers, the Canadian unemployed, in short the Canadian families which also need food and perhaps industrial machinery on the eastern farms.
For instance, we are told that Japan is improving greatly, that Hiroshima was built following its destruction, and so on. However, we are not being told about the number of unemployed in Japan. Perhaps there are not any? If so, why are we not given the reasons for it, so that we could adopt the same methods in Canada and improve the living conditions of Canadians?
It seems to me that it is high time for the ministers, who travel throughout the world, to submit to us concrete and objective solutions which would set our own house in order. We could then bring this to bear on our relations with neighbouring countries.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON MEETING OF COMMONWEALTH ECONOMIC CONSULTATIVE COUNCIL
speechtext:
On the way to Kuala Lumpur we paid short visits to Hong Kong and Singapore, meeting local government officials and businessmen interested in trade with Canada. While in Hong Kong we had the opportunity of discussions with representatives of the China Resources Company which, as hon. members are aware, has been buying substantial quantities of wheat from the Canadian wheat board on behalf of mainland China.
In Hong Kong, in Singapore, in Kuala Lumpur and later in Tokyo we were enormously impressed by the high rate of economic activity. Everywhere one looked factories were being erected, roads were being built, apartment houses were rising. There can be no doubt that these Pacific countries are on the march and have great potential as markets for Canadian products.
Inquiries of the Ministry
The commonwealth economic consultative council met in Kuala Lumpur on the first anniversary of the founding of Malaysia. We were happy to join in the celebrations. I regret to say that the celebrations were marred by less happy events, and I draw attention to the text of the communique in which the ministers from all the 18 independent commonwealth countries joined in recalling the assurance given by the commonwealth prime ministers of their sympathy and support of Malaysia's efforts to preserve its sovereign independence and integrity and to achieve a peaceful and honourable settlement of its current differences with its neighbours.
The discussions at Kuala Lumpur were notable for their emphasis upon the problems of the developing countries, both within and without the commonwealth. We were happy to be able to say that Canada is stepping up the level and quality of our external aid, particularly in the field of education, and that the government of Canada supports strongly the international efforts that are being made to improve the trading position of the developing countries.

The house resumed, from Thursday, September 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Churchill.

Mr. Speaker, if I may resume from where I left
Canadian Flag
off last Thursday evening when 10.30 was called, I was speaking in this debate for the first time since the flag resolution was brought before the house. I mentioned that the Canadian people are actually wondering now what is going on in the parliament of Canada. They are wondering, as I said last Thursday, whether we are a bunch of school kids who have lost our teacher. They do not seem to get any guidance whatever from this parliament at the moment, either on the flag issue or on government business, because the only business we are considering at the moment is the flag. I am under the impression that today we are further away from a Canadian flag than we ever were before. At least before we started this debate there seemed to me a mutual understanding that Canada wanted a flag, but at the stage we have now reached the people are wondering whether they should have a flag; parliament itself has not decided whether they should have a flag or whether the people should vote on it. The people are wondering whether this flag will unite Canada or divide it. At the moment things are moving in such direction that it is dividing Canada instead of uniting us.
We must ask ourselves, Mr. Speaker: What does this flag stand for. If it is going to stand for the ripping of Canada into parts, either regional, provincial or as a nation itself, we may as well not have a flag at all. We want a flag, as do all Canadians, which will not only stand for one group, one religion, one race or one nation, but for Canada; a flag to represent Canada among the other nations of the world as a united and strong nation. The flag should represent all of our historical background and proclaim our unity. It should stand for the social security which we have in Canada. It should stand for individual freedom and for the freedom of any association which exists within its boundaries.
Everyone is proud to look at a flag which stands for something; but what a disgrace it would be if when we looked at our Canadian flag we had to say it is that flag which has destroyed the nation itself. If we do not want that we must play our part as the responsible elected members of this nation, judge the situation as objectively as possible, and take part in this debate using the greatest wisdom we can deploy. If we do not do that it will be the downfall perhaps not only of the government but of confederation and the nation as it stands.
I might have used some very harsh words, Mr. Speaker, last Thursday night when I spoke of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS
Canadian Flag
Diefenbaker) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson); but believe me I think they are true. It is up to the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of the government to take their responsibility as the two great leaders in this nation. Remember, Mr. Speaker, that the Leader of the Opposition is regarded as just as important as the Prime Minister himself in the form of government we have. It is up to the Leader of the Opposition to bring forward any constructive objections which he has as to why why we should have or should not have such a flag. But it is not the responsibility of the Leader of the Opposition to create any kind of obstruction in such a situation, whether good or bad. The role of the government as well as the opposition-any opposition-is to judge what is best for the Canadian nation, because we are here to represent Canadian interests, not our own.
We have had all kinds of speeches, Mr. Speaker, and some very good ones. They might not always have related to the subject as we would wish, and I myself sometimes stray in that regard; but we are all trying to have our say. I am wondering however, whether we are all trying to find a solution. It is not only a matter of speaking and then sitting down and saying we have done our job. We should speak in such a way that we might find a solution which will take this parliament out of the mess it is in today, a mess brought on by ourselves and nobody else.
The Canadian people were told in the last election campaign that the Liberal party would take a stand on a Canadian flag. Therefore it is up to us, as the responsible elected representatives of the people, to be their spokesmen. Let us carry out this task wisely and justly, and try to do it in such a way that we will save the nation, not destroy it. The Conservative members have objections to this flag resolution. They have brought in some amendments, but I have seen no reference to the flag on the amendments. It is now or never, Mr. Speaker; we cannot delay any longer. We desire unity but we will not accept unity with uniformity. We do not expect that any member of this house or Canadian citizen would accept unity on that basis. We will accept, however, unity with diversity, because that is the only democratic method to be followed. Every citizen of this country should have the opportunity of expressing an opinion in respect of this flag, and that is the only way
[Mr. Langlois.l
we can follow the majority rule principle. Such a selection by majority rule would be acceptable to everyone, provided it did not ignore the basic rights of any minority or individual.
As a young member of parliament looking at the situation which has developed in this house, Mr. Speaker, I am ashamed in public to admit that I am a member of parliament. The situation with which we are now faced is shameful. We have expressed our opinions. We have fought for what we believe is right. We believe that Canada has a history comparable to that of any other country in the world. Canadians can be proud of what has been obtained and attained through sacrifice, valour and hard work. Our ancestors should be commended for what they have accomplished in this regard, and it is up to us in this house to continue the progress of this nation, rather than to destroy it as we are doing through a continuation of this debate. I think everyone now has come to the realization that we have now reached the crossroads and must act quickly. We cannot permit ourselves to continue to be a group of asses listening to ourselves bray. We have done too much of this already. At this time we must find a solution acceptable to all parties in this house. Each member of each party in this House of Commons is an elected representative of the people, and each opinion must be respected.
It is not my intention to raise further objections or points which might rekindle the flame of debate, but we must soon settle on some plausible solution to the problems which now exist. The Liberal government has presented its idea in respect of the flag, that being the three maple leaf design embodied in the main motion. Other suggestions have been made, and we have all seen various proposed designs. I have one before me at the moment, prepared by Jean Dubuc, who is a descendant of the man who wrote the words of "O Canada". I do not know how close a relative he is, but one of his ancestors certainly did write those words.
Whether we accept the design proposed by the government, or another design, we must have a flag which will stand for national unity, and will be looked upon with pride by Canadians. There is nothing which tears my heart more, as well as the heart of anyone else in this house, or any Canadian citizen, than does the suggestion that we will need a special type of vehicle to protect the Queen on her visit to this country. I think we must begin to protect Canadians generally in view

of the situation that is now developing. Many people are beginning to tear out their hair because this flag debate continues without any indication of conclusion, and because all the time it continues it divides this country and whatever unity does exist. As long as we continue to beat around the bush here in this house, without coming to any plausible solution to the problem, we are going to further this division. We have now been debating this flag issue for 22 days, and talked about it as early as last spring, without any good result. As a matter of fact, I am now under the impression that we are further away from a solution than we have ever been, and if we continue to follow the course we have followed we will divide this House of Commons into groups, and this country into ethnic associations.
The United Nations, made up of representatives of almost every country in this world, was able to adopt a flag within a very short period of time. Why cannot we decide upon a flag in a similar fashion which will represent the two founding races of this country and those Canadians of other ethnic origin who have come to this country adopting its customs and rules, and who, I am sure, will adopt its flag when and if the Canadian government presents one that is acceptable and representative of unity? Let us put our political feelings aside while dealing with this issue. It is useless to attempt to save our own skins at the expense of national unity because our skins would not be worth much without a country.
A day or two ago I heard an hon. member state that debate is the living right of parliament. I admit that fact, but on this occasion it might well prove to be the death of our Canadian nation. We do desire a Canadian flag, but let us have one that will stand for unity. I am sure the Canadian economy has suffered and will suffer more because of the time lost by this parliament during the debate on this flag issue. This parliament is now behind in its normal work. We did not have a budget presented to the house for several years. We are now losing a great deal of time by discussing the type of flag Canada should adopt, and by the time we do come to some conclusion this nation will be divided and the flag will then be useless because it will stand for little or nothing.
I should like at this time, Mr. Speaker, to present possible solution to our problems, and outline my understanding of the situation. I think it is much easier for a small group of members, perhaps 15, to come to
Division
some agreement in respect of a flag design than it would be for the 265 members in this house. Each of the 265 members, in expressing individual and representative points of view, will tend to keep us apart just long enough to destroy whatever unity we now have. I think a small committee could work together discussing the situation objectively, and arrive at some plausible and acceptable solution upon which we could vote to accept or reject.
I do not intend to speak any longer on this flag issue because I feel that the sooner I conclude my remarks the sooner we will find an acceptable solution to our problems. I suggest that this house should adjourn this debate today for a period of 60 days, referring this resolution to a committee comprised of 15 members; seven from the Liberal party, five from the Conservative party, one from the New Democratic party, one from the Social Credit party and one from the Ralliement Creditiste. This 15 member committee could discuss the matter for 60 days starting from today. Then the resolution could be brought back to this house and debated for a period, let us say of six days, somewhat like the throne speech debate or the budget debate. There could be a limit of six days. Then there could be a vote. If it did not pass, nothing would be destroyed; we could go back on the flag debate. However in the meantime the house would have an opportunity of dealing with something else and taking care of the Canadian people. I believe the committee would have a better opportunity of finding a solution to this matter than we would have in this house.
I move therefore, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), that this debate do now adjourn.
I declare the motion lost.

Mr. Speaker, I can understand the right hon. gentleman's feeling of frustration, when only 44 members of his party were here; but I am at a loss to understand his irritation at being delayed from attending what he himself used to refer to ironically as an egghead conference. Mr. Speaker, I think the vote which has taken place indicates quite clearly the concern of the house regarding prolonging the debate on the flag issue and the imperative need for our trying to find some solution to the stalemate in which parliament finds itself. This debate started on June 15 and it has continued since that time, with an interruption for several pieces of legislation. But it has gone on continuously for the past five weeks, with the exception of the one day each week which is set aside for the discussion of estimates. Now we are embarking on the sixth week of debating this matter.
Tell us something we don't know.

Mr. Speaker, I hear someone from the Conservative party asking me to tell them something they don't know. I do not

know that I can tell them something they don't know, but I can tell them what I think an increasing number of people in this country know, namely that the reason for this prolonged debate is the fact that the Conservative party in this house seems to be determined to keep parliament from reaching a decision.
Hear, hear.
We don't accept that at all.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, this is rather significant. For five weeks we have been debating this question, and the major part of the time has been taken up by the Conservative party. They have constantly appealed to other people to participate in the debate, and the moment those other members do so they are heckled and interrupted by the hon. gentlemen who sit on my right.
Hear, hear.

It seems to me it is a sign of weakness in one's defence when constantly he has to keep someone else from presenting his point of view. I had hoped, sitting through these five weeks of debate without taking any part, that after members had expressed their point of view we would be allowed to reach a decision; but last week it became increasingly apparent that the official opposition were going to keep moving innocuous subamendments in order to prevent not only the house reaching a decision on their amendment but to prevent other parties in this house moving amendments upon which the house could make a decision. I suggest that this is a negation of democratic government.
A great deal has been said by some speakers about the government seeking to ram a flag down their throats. I would point out in the first place that the present government is a minority government. The government has not a clear majority in the house and the French Canadian members have not a clear majority in the house. Therefore no flag can be rammed down people's throats unless the majority of the members are prepared to vote for it. I think the members should be given an opportunity to vote for it at a fairly early stage.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I have listened patiently for five weeks to the opinions expressed by the members of the official opposition against the maple leaf flag design, either that proposed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) or the single maple leaf design which
Canadian Flag
we have indicated it is our intention to place before the house. I respect the views of those who have put up arguments, and I should like to take the three main lines of argument which have been used as to why some hon. members are against a maple leaf design.
The first is that they say this maple leaf design is a concession to Quebec.
No.

They have either said that themselves or have quoted other people who have said it, and said it in most intemperate and immoderate terms. Someone says no; well I am not going to weary the house, unless I am pressed to, by going over the speeches of hon. members. I have gone over them carefully each day and I can quote for hon. members chapter and verse the speeches which have been made saying specifically that this flag is a concession to Quebec; that this is something which the government is using to get votes in Quebec. The record is clear for anyone who wants to examine it, and if necessary I am prepared to take time, either now or later in the debate, to put all these quotes on Hansard; there are pages of them. Suffice it to say for the moment that I think this kind of argument is hurting national unity and if it is persisted in it will wreck confederation. And, may I say, it will wreck the Conservative party.
I would point out that there Eire no French symbols on the flag which has been proposed. There are no French symbols in the maple leaf design. French Canada has not asked for them because they are sufficiently mature to recognize that in this situation Canada must be concerned about the present and the future rather than being obsessed with the divisions of the past.
The second line of argument which has been presented is that by not having the union jack on the flag we are removing the Christian symbols. I should like to point out that the crosses in the union jack are not Christian symbols in the true sense of the word.
Oh yes, they are.

They represent battle banners which were used; St. George's cross was first used in the crusade when the kings, barons and knights of Christendom perpetrated murder, rapine and plunder in the name of Christianity; the flag of St. Andrew was first used by the Piets and the Scots in their wars against the Saxons; the cross of St. Patrick was on the banner of the Fitzpatricks when

Canadian Flag
they conquered Ireland, and very few Irishmen will be crying for the cross of St. Patrick. Certainly it has never been adopted as Ireland's flag.
Let us remember first of all that Christianity is not the only faith in Canada. There are people of Jewish faith, the Mohammedan faith and the Buddhist faith.
And the communist faith.
Well, I will leave that to my hon. friend.
Is that not true?

He can speak for some of his friends; I am speaking for mine at the moment. But I submit that in the flags which have been proposed-either the three maple leaf design, the single maple leaf design which we have been advancing, or the design proposed by A. Y. Jackson more than 50 years ago-you have blue bands which do have a religious significance because they are a constant reminder that our motto "From sea to sea" was based on the eighth verse of the 72nd psalm:
He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.
This design has a religious significance not peculiarly Christian but of general application to the Christian-Judean faiths-that the things of God should have priority in the lives of our people from one coast of Canada to another.
The third objection which has been taken to the maple leaf design is that it is removing the symbols of our British connections. All of us are proud of the fact, especially those of us of British origin, that Britain has played such an important role in Canadian history. We are convinced that this influence will live on in our democratic institutions. It will live most meaningfully if we make those institutions work, and work effectively. I submit that it is a sign of political immaturity to refuse to cut the apron strings and walk out on our own feet. It is still true to say:
Daughter am I in my mother's house;
But mistress in my own.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that those who keep talking about the union jack, the battle of Hastings and British history should forget that we cannot go back into the womb of the past. There comes a time when any independent nation must cut the umbilical cord and step out on its own. This debate, which has been going on now for all these weeks, reminds me of the discussions we heard 20 to 25 years ago, when a former

member for North Battleford, a man called Cameron R. McIntosh, used to bring in a resolution each year for a national flag for Canada. He proposed the red ensign, and I remember all the speeches which were made in favour of the union jack. In 1946, when the government of Mackenzie King passed an order in council saying that the red ensign should be flown on public buildings-
It was 1945.

Yes, that is correct; September 1945-at that time I was associated with a provincial administration, and every year for many years delegations came to wait on the government to protest over the flag we were flying, the red ensign, and saying that by refusing to fly the union jack we were denying our connection with the motherland; that we were being false to the blood in our veins. All of the arguments that were used then against the red ensign are now being used for the red ensign.
I have no disrespect, Mr. Speaker, for the union jack. I would be the last person to be disrespectful to it because I was born under it. It is a great flag with a great tradition. But I did not come to Canada to build another little Britain, or little Scotland, or another little England. I came to this country to help build Canada, in which the British traditions of which I am so proud, along with the contributions and the cultures of other ethnic groups and races, could come together to enrich this new country. Therefore, if we are to have that kind of country, this flag must be a symbol of our hopes and aspirations for the future-namely, a united people who are seeking to establish a Canadian identity on this North American continent. I think I have made it clear that as far as I am concerned I have not been convinced by the arguments against the maple leaf design.
Let me turn now to the other side of the question. The government has manoeuvred itself into a political and parliamentary impasse. When I spoke during this debate on June 16 I made the statement that I thought the government had chosen the wrong time and the wrong method to introduce the flag question. We felt that, with all the legislative program before us, a matter like a flag ought not to be introduced at a time when it was almost certain to block the passage of that legislative program. We also felt there should have been some other method by which we could obtain a consensus about a flag, rather than putting a specific design to the House of Commons

where it was almost certain to become a bone of contention.
We in this party, or at least, the great majority of us, are prepared to support a maple leaf design, but I think it is equally apparent that the English speaking section of one of the major political parties is in apparent disagreement and has now embarked upon a policy of obstruction. I think we have to face that fact and have to deal with it. I think we have to begin by remembering that dealing with a flag issue is not the same as dealing with a legislative matter. If this were a matter of some important legislative significance, there are parliamentary means of bringing the matter to a decision. In respect of this question, even if we could force a decision, it would be a Pyrrhic decision. A flag adopted by Canada should represent the consensus, and should be launched with the general support of the vast majority of the Canadian people. It should be an instrument for forging unity rather than creating division, and no flag will accomplish that if it is conceived in controversy and born in bitterness. This would be equally true, in my opinion, if we were trying to force the red ensign through this house. I think therefore that in this situation the government has three courses left open to it. The first course is, it can dissolve this parliament and call an election. I hope members will believe me when I say I am not opposed to an election on this issue because I have any fear from the standpoint of this political party. I think we could do rather well in an election where the bankruptcy of statesmanship on the part of the two old line parties has become so apparent. I am not concerned about an election, I am concerned about Canada. I believe that this country would suffer irreparable damage, irrespective of the outcome of the election. I think any election on the flag issue would divide the country on racial grounds, which would split confederation, and even if confederation survived it would take a quarter of a century to heal the scars that would result.
Therefore, I say I think members in all parts of the house, or some of them at least, will agree that there should be no irresponsible action taken by either side of this house by any political party which would result in such a catastrophe.
The government has a second choice. It could force a decision by closure, or by a war of attrition. To my mind the former is unthinkable, particularly in respect of so emotionally charged a question as the flag issue. To launch a new flag for Canada by means
Canadian Flag
of a closure motion would mean launching a new flag with resentment and bitterness in the hearts of a very considerable section of the Canadian people. The latter course, a war of attrition, would mean that we would neglect a legislative program which ought to be dealt with, and dealt with speedily.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent) made a statement on Thursday evening to the effect that no legislation should be passed, no estimates passed and no money voted to this government until this question was settled by referring it to the people. I do not know whether he was speaking for his party or only for himself, but if that is the course to be followed, then prolonging the debate by a war of attrition will mean that we will do little or nothing by way of constructive legislation at this session. If that attitude is going to be taken, and I have made it clear that I do not condone it, I think we must reconcile ourselves to the fact that we are either going to have no flag at all, or a flag at the price of bitterness and hard feelings, which is not in my opinion a good way to launch an emblem that is to fly proudly over this nation.
Therefore, the third solution, which is the only choice the government has left, is that the government must find some type of compromise out of this difficulty. I readily acknowledge to the Prime Minister that the government has made the major concessions, and almost the only concessions that have been made on this issue. The government has agreed to a free vote, so that an election is not hanging on the outcome.
Oh, oh.

There is no point to the laughter of my friends in the Conservative ranks, because they continually asked for a free vote, and if they were doing so seriously they ought to be serious in appreciating the fact that this concession has been made.
The government has agreed that it was not wedded to any one design, and that it is up to this house in the final analysis to choose a design, providing it is a distinctive national flag which cannot be mistaken for the flag of any other country.
The Prime Minister agreed to the establishment of a committee, as did every other political leader except the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), and to send this matter to that committee subject to the proviso that there be a time limit on the debate on the committee's report. The government has made some concessions, and I am suggesting now that in the present situation we must

Canadian Flag
be prepared to explore the situation further. I realize some will argue that if we do this we are knuckling under to blackmail from the official opposition. In the kind of stalemate in which we find ourselves we have to be prepared to make concessions in an attempt to find some common ground. After all, the government must accept responsibility for the fact that this matter is before us. They are the ones who introduced it, and they must have known when they introduced it that it would be a controversial matter, and would not go through the house easily. We really are in the position of trench warfare, in which both sides have dug in and every day which passes during this debate, they are digging in a little deeper. We are faced with a hopeless stalemate. The only hope lies in a major breakthrough so that the house can get some freedom of movement from which some positive decision can be made.
I want to suggest we try a compromise proposal. I suggest that we pick up where we left off in the statements that were made by the leaders of all the political parties in the house on Friday, August 21. I am not speaking of the suggestions that were made by the party leaders in their conferences. I am talking about statements that were made by the party leaders in this house on the order for motions on August 21. I suggest we pick up from there and see where we disagree, see if there is some loophole by which we can find common ground.
I am proposing briefly three things. One is, as was suggested, that a parliamentary committee composed of 15 members be established, seven from the government, five from the official opposition and one from each of the other political parties. I think such a committee ought to have the help of heraldic experts. This is my first suggestion.
The second suggestion is that the committee should report back to the house within 60 days. This time limit could be negotiated. If the Prime Minister would like it shorter or the Leader of the Opposition would like it longer, I think that matter could be negotiated and could be discussed in the party leaders' meeting. I think that in a matter as important as this, 15 days one way or the other is not going to make any difference. We have been able to get along for 100 years without a flag, so if by waiting 20 days more we can find an answer, let us not bother about that. I am suggesting, for negotiating purposes, 60 days.
The third suggestion is that when the committee's report is ready there should be an-

other meeting of the party leaders to determine the length of time that should be devoted in the house to a discussion of the committee's report. While I personally believe that there should be a time limit agreed upon in advance, I would be willing to defer this decision until after the committee's report is ready in order to reach agreement and set up the committee.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I know all the advantages and disadvantages of the proposal. I know it would be much better if we could agree in advance as to how long this debate would take when the committee reported back. It has been suggested that if there were a certain percentage, it would be so long; for other percentages, it would be longer. I do not believe you are going to get agreement on that in advance. It seems to me there is much to be said for sending this matter to the committee, having the committee report back in 60 days and just before they report the party leaders could meet. If there were 12 members out of 15 in agreement on the report, then we should be able to arrange for a very short debate. If there were a severe difference of opinion, then it might not be so easy to get agreement about a time limit. Why not let us leave that question until we see how the committee gets along?
Now, let me try to anticipate the reactions to this proposal. I think the Leader of the Opposition should be willing to endorse the suggestion I am making because it falls in line, to some extent, with the proposals which he made in the house on August 21 as recorded at page 7112 of Hansard. Now, the Prime Minister would be more justified in having some reservations about accepting this proposal because he, like myself and the leader of the other political parties, has argued for a time limit to be set in advance, that is a time limit on the debate on the committee's report. Those of us who took that position on August 21 did so because we felt that if we did not have a time limit on the debate on the committee's report we could find ourselves, 60 days from now, just where we are today. This is the argument I put up in the house on August 21.
I want to argue now that by deferring the decision as to limiting the time of the debate, we would still be making some gains. We would not be as badly off as we are today. First of all, in the meantime, we would have been able to spend eight weeks on legislative work in the house. We would have been able to get some legislation passed. We would have been able to get on with the country's

business. I hear somebody say, "We might get holidays". I think the holiday time has gone; we are here to work. I thank my friends to the right for the only holidays we are likely to get. I think now we should get on with the country's business; that is what the people of Canada are demanding, get on with the business. Eight weeks from now, therefore, we would at least be this far ahead. We would have some legislation on the statute books. If this included the Canada pension plan, we would be very happy.
The second thing is that my proposals have this advantage. We have at least a reasonable prospect-I think a 50-50 prospect-that the committee might come up with a solution. The Leader of the Opposition has said publicly that he would be prepared to co-operate by selecting representatives from his party who have not taken an inflexible position on the flag issue. If he follows that course and the other parties follow a similar course of action, we might get a committee that would work out a solution. It would be worth a try. I know this, there is a better chance of 15 members trying to find a solution behind closed doors than there is for 265 members trying to find it in the glare of publicity. It might not work, but it is worth a chance. We have nothing to lose.
The third advantage of this proposal is that it would have demonstrated to the Canadian people that parliament is sufficiently flexible to meet a situation that calls for statesmanship. Make no mistake about it, Mr. Speaker, the real casualty in a cold war of attrition will be parliament itself. The responsibility for this lies with the two major political parties. It is often said, a little contemptuously sometimes, that the smaller parties are the reason we cannot get on with the business of this parliament; the smaller parties are the reason there is no efficiency in parliament. You cannot blame the three smaller parties in this instance. We did not initiate this issue and we have not prolonged this issue. We have been ready at all times to take a vote and bring this matter to a decision. It has been the two old line parties who have been like two old bulls in a pasture butting their heads together. They must accept the responsibility for the stalemate in which we find ourselves. We think that the time has come to end this cold war of attrition and seek a solution before we do irreparable damage to parliament and to confederation.
If I may just in closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that the Prime Minister may feel he will be accused of beating a 20220-489

retreat if he accepts this proposal. I can understand that fear because of some of the jibes that have been hurled at him from time to time. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that it takes a man of stature to make a concession in the interests of national unity; any pipsqueak can stubbornly cling to a position long after it is untenable. I think the Prime Minister of this country can, and I think he will demonstrate the kind of stature that is necessary to give this country the leadership it needs in this difficult time.
If a compromise is reached by all parties along the lines I have suggested, it will not be a decision taken solely by the Prime Minister. On August 21 I, and the leaders of other groups, except the Leader of the Opposition, argued for having a time limit on the debate of the committee's report. I am prepared to defer the decision about a time limit until after the committee's report is ready. If anyone wants to say I am retreating, he may do so. I am not afraid of being accused of backing down. I am concerned not so much with chalking up debating points as I am concerned with finding a solution without sacrifice of principle, and I do not believe it is beyond the ingenuity of this house to work out a compromise and an accommodation.
Therefore I am urging the Prime Minister to consider calling a meeting of the party leaders if there is any indication that the proposal I have outlined is acceptable to the other parties as a starting point for negotiations. The reason I did not get up the other day when the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) urged the Prime Minister to call another meeting is that unless there is some change of attitude, unless there is some new proposal to be considered I do not see any value in such a meeting. But if the various leaders feel the suggestion I have made about a committee, with a 60 day limitation, with the question of the limit of debate on its report to be left until the report is ready-if they feel this offers some basis for discussion, then I would urge the Prime Minister to call such a meeting.
After all, Mr. Speaker, the leaders of this house are the Prime Minister of Canada and a former prime minister of Canada. In the final analysis the solution depends on their willingness to co-operate. When we are selecting a national symbol, a flag that is to be the emblem of Canada, it must have the support of at least the major part of the two largest parties in the house, and it seems to me that the answer lies in finding some

Canadian Flag
common ground between these two gentlemen.
One hundred years ago Sir John A. Macdonald and George Brown laid aside their differences in order to bring Canadian confederation into birth. I am appealing to the two leaders of this house to follow the same course now in order to strengthen the bonds of confederation at a time when they are sorely strained. If they fail to respond then Canada will be the poorer, but if they succeed future generations will applaud them.
I say to both the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, and indeed to every member of parliament, we have a great opportunity to put posterity in our debt and to so conduct ourselves that future generations will be able to say we matched the challenge of the troubled times in which we lived.

May I ask the hon. member a question. In the event that substantial agreement could be reached in less time than 60 days, say in one week, two weeks or three weeks, does he mean that the committee could bring in its report prior to the time limit placed on it, in order that agreement be brought about more quickly?

I think the term I used was within 60 days. Maybe I should have used the term not later than 60 days. If the committee could reach a decision within two or three weeks, then certainly let it bring in its report, but if it cannot reach a decision within 60 days any further discussion by the committee would serve no useful purpose.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to prolong the debate unduly because I think that the sorry spectacle the house is now giving to the Canadian people is not to the credit of our parliamentary system, far from it.
I support wholeheartedly what the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas) has just said. That does not mean that I support all his political ideas, because I am at the very opposite of state socialism, and will be for a long time. However, I think it should be said that the spirit which permeates the speech the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has just made is truly Canadian. The hon. member was not speaking as an English speaking or a French speaking Canadian but as a Canadian. We hope that the day will come when each member of parliament will speak as a Canadian instead of trying, as the Conservatives have been

doing for two months, to create division, a division which increases day after day throughout Canada.
We saw the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) go to Winnipeg two months ago, to meet the Canadian Legion and face, I would not say animosity, but feelings which were really difficult and hard for a government and for a Prime Minister who had stated at that time that we ought to have a distinctive national flag.
I said then that the Prime Minister had acted like a head of state by meeting those people who, on a particular point, were strongly hostile. But when the Prime Minister came back to the house, he acted not like a head of state but like a diplomat. There is a difference between a diplomat and a head of state. I see that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) is paying attention to what I am saying, because he does know the difference. A head of state must make decisions, while the diplomat endeavours to smooth things over and acts as a conciliator between the various groups.
The Prime Minister acted or tried to act like a diplomat by moving a resolution including two flags. That is the reason for the debate which has been going on.
If the Prime Minister had put before the house a resolution involving only one Canadian flag-not a French flag, or an English flag or the flag of the province of Quebec or the flag of British Columbia, but one flag for all Canada, with a Canadian symbol-I am positive that the flag would have been passed within five or six days. But the resolution gave rise to this debate which, at the very outset, led us to splitting the resolution. You made a ruling yourself, Mr. Speaker, saying that the resolution would be divided into A and B, that part A would concern the distinctive national flag, while part B would concern the union jack.
Here again, that is the point on which the Conservatives take their stand to boycott and filibuster from the beginning of the debate on this matter of a distinctive national flag. That is the basis of the Conservative arguments, which is unfortunate.
As I said before, and as the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam just stated, the impression has been created in Canada that the distinctive national flag is intended to please Quebec whereas the union jack is intented to please English speaking Canadians. Now, there is no question of a distinctive national flag being only designed to

please the province of Quebec because, if that was the case, I would ask the Prime Minister not to introduce it, because we already have one and we do not need a second one. One is enough. But we Quebeckers are ready, not as French Canadians but as Canadians, to approve any distinctive flag project for Canada, something which would belong to the ten Canadian provinces and not to one alone.
The Conservative filibuster has been reported in the press and been abundantly used on television and all mass media.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) is still accusing us today of hatching a plot with the Liberal party in order to ram a flag down the throat of the Canadian people.
At the time the leaders of the five parties met and the fact was mentioned that the Prime Minister was accepting a free vote in the house-and at this stage I may say that the Prime Minister made concession upon concession so as to reach an understanding and to give Canadians a distinctive national flag-the Leader of the Opposition stuck to his guns and refused to accept the concession and to agree to a settlement. We had gathered together and the free vote question was mentioned.
Mr. Speaker, nobody can make me believe that I am a member of the Liberal party. I am not; neither is the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Thompson) nor the leader of the New Democratic party. However, in the interest of national unity and for the good of Canadians in general, we were ready to end those fights which serve no purpose and to stop calling forth phantoms to scare the people or to divide even further the various groups which constitute the Canadian nation. We felt that a free vote would enable a majority of hon. members to express their opinion, that such a majority would naturally represent the majority of Canadian electors who have sent us to parliament to take decisions not to talk through our hats or filibuster as the Conservatives have been doing for the past two or three weeks.
At the time, we spoke of a majority decision but the Leader of the Opposition objected on the grounds that a majority of members would be imposing a distinctive national flag on a minority. On the other hand, the Leader of the Opposition was proposing the red ensign with a fleur-de-lis in the bottom and a union jack at the top; he was ready to force his design on six million French Canadians in the province of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether he was honest and sincere when he proposed that compromise or that procedure on the flag issue.
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the official opposition was persistent in his ideas and refused to accept the proposals made by the Prime Minister or the other party leaders during these meetings. Mr. Speaker, I was beginning to wonder whether I would ever get the floor tonight. In the

remaining moments left to me this evening I should like to begin my remarks with what are my sincere comments on this issue. This evening has been quite interesting and I am sure the gallery must have been regaled with the antics of the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis). After seeing and listening to him there is no question in my mind why he remains a minister without a portfolio. He began his remarks with very profuse congratulations to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) for the very high level of his remarks this afternoon. What a pity he does not follow that rule himself. The speeches he delivers in this house-indeed, the type of speech I have heard him deliver on each occasion he speaks in the house-are anything but on a high level. He chose to quote a number of references from Hansard of 1961, which purported to be statements by hon. members in this party in which they had stated that they were in favour of a distinctive national flag. I do not think there is any conflict there, any more than there is now. I am sure that most hon. members in this house are in favour of a distinctive national flag. I say "a distinctive national flag", not two or three flags as proposed by hon. members opposite. It is not a question whether or not we are opposed to or in favour of a distinctive national flag. This is not the point at issue right now. What we are opposed to, and I think what Canadians generally across the country are opposed to, is the anaemic, insipid design which has been proposed by this government. If a flag is to be distinctive and is to be Canadian, then it must be one which meets with the approval of all Canadians.
I was also interested in the new theory of democracy propounded by the Minister without Portfolio when he stated that he thought that because government members and those who support them were in the majority, the opposition should simply quit talking and allow the resolution to come to a vote. What an example of how little he knows about parliamentary government. In my opinion it is a disgrace for a minister of the crown to stand on his feet in this house and put forward such theories and express such thoughts.
This debate, which has gone on for the past few days, has certainly generated a certain amount of heat. Perhaps tonight was the best example of how much heat has been generated. I am not going to make any comments about the light that was shed, but it was at least most entertaining. If the debate has done nothing else I think it is making Canadians

across this country aware of our history. It is making Canadians aware of what a flag means to this country. It is making Canadians think about designs for a flag. As a result of this debate I think there will be a greater participation on the part of the Canadian people in the national affairs of the country. I do not suggest that the people who have spoken in this debate are accurately reflecting the views of all Canadians, but most certainly those who have spoken have made statements and expressed feelings which I am sure are expressed by somebody. Even the comments made by the Minister without Portfolio will be received, I dare say, by somebody in this country. I think it is the responsibility of members of parliament to express these feelings, because if we are to be a true reflection of the attitudes and thoughts of Canadians across the country, then those attitudes and thoughts must be expressed in this house.
It has been suggested that Canadians generally are getting tired of this debate. I am sure most hon. members discussed this issue over the Labour day week end with their constituents. I am sure that most of our constituents feel that the debate has gone on far longer than it needed to go on. But at the same time those of my constituents who have said to me that they think the debate has gone on too long have followed that remark up very quickly by saying: "But you simply must not allow this insipid design to be passed". So what other method is there open to the opposition? What other method is there open to a member of parliament to prevent the government's foisting this folly upon the Canadian people, other than debating the matter in the house, and debating it to the point where the government realize that the people of this country are not going to be happy with this design?
Another thing which has contributed to this feeling among Canadians is the fact that from the time the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) made his first statement to the Canadian Legion convention in Winnipeg, this issue has been played up by the newspapers across the country. I do not criticize the newspapers for this because their job is to sell newspapers and they do that the best way they can. But none the less the feeling has got abroad that nothing has been done in this house since early April, when the Prime Minister spoke to the Legion con-
Canadian Flag
vention in Winnipeg. That is not the case. These sensational headlines with which we have been greeted day after day since before the resolution was introduced have certainly created in the minds of the people across the country the impression that this issue was on the floor of the House of Commons long before it was in fact presented to the house.
I think that if Canadians are tired of the debate on this issue they are even more tired of this government-this dismal, abject failure of a government. To quote the words of Peter Newman it is a quiet, grey failure of a government which has fumbled and failed to bring to a conclusion every policy it has introduced in this house. It has failed to come to grips with the economic problems of this country, and it is really the economic problems which are paramount. In fact, the government is trying to cover up the real difficulties with this issue. I remember, when we were the government, how they ridiculed almost every measure we brought forward, but it is strange today that those measures which we introduced have now become law in this country without change. Indeed, they have been carried on very proudly by some members of the present government.
When the present government's minister of finance presented the three budgets, which met with some considerable agitation, certainly the image of decisiveness disappeared and, I might add, never returned. I am sure members will recall how the present government boasted that it would improve our relations with the United States. I recall reading a comment in a New York newspaper to the effect that if the Pearson government is a friend of the United States, who needs enemies. I recall how the government said it would improve relations with the provinces. We only have to think back to the measures that have been introduced respecting dominion-provincial relations to realize that-
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak to a point of order. I wonder whether you would ask the hon. member to relate his remarks to the resolution now before us.

Of course I am happy to do so. The subamendment deals with the question of national unity, and all the things

Canadian Flag
I have mentioned are part and parcel of that subject. Can you deny that relations with provinces, including the province of Quebec, constitute a question of national unity?
I am sure that the majority of hon. members in this house are aware of the so-called quiet revolution taking place in Quebec. I do not think we need fear it. I think perhaps it is a good thing for this country, because these people are attempting to find their place in confederation and do the things necessary for them to be a part and remain a part of this country. The problems that beset the province of Quebec are largely economical and must be dealt with by economic measures. This government has failed miserably to introduce anything that could possibly be of benefit to the province of Quebec, other than by continuing the policies initiated by the former government, particularly as they relate to ARDA.
I wonder what happened to the policy in respect to two ministers of agriculture. I suggest everything that this government has done has tended to create division, including the establishment of the bilingualism and bicul-turalism probe. This government seems bound to aggravate and destroy the unity that existed when it came into office, and in order to cover up its failure to deal with these problems it has attempted to divert attention by proposing the two flag resolution. This government has attempted to confuse the issue, and to convince the citizens of the province of Quebec that it is doing great things for them, when in reality it is doing nothing to solve the economic problems that beset that province.
Very frequently during this debate we have heard hon. members opposite ask for cessation of the debate. They have often said, bring this to a vote and let us end it all; let the members of the House of Commons decide this issue. They make these statements as though such a decision would really solve anything, surely those members are not so naive as to think that if a vote was taken in this house it would end the problem. Certainly they should know, and would know if they had
gone home over the last week end, that a vote would not solve the problem or end the debate. It would end the debate in the House of Commons, but not the debate that is taking place across this country.
Mr. Speaker, one of the best editorials I have read on this particular subject appeared in the Ottawa Journal of August 31, 1964, and I should like to put it on record. The editorial, headed "Not Speed but a Flag", reads as follows:
The Commons is confusing the challenge the flag debate presents.
The real task is to produce a flag that will unite a nation.
Whether that takes a month or four months is relatively unimportant.
An error is not less so if it is done quickly.
Mr. Pearson speaks of a month's debate over-all; Mr. Diefenbaker speaks of three months in committee plus a final Commons debate on approval.
We must be wary now lest we think the goal is simply to narrow that time gap. The goal is a flag that will please most Canadians.
Mr. Diefenbaker is not resisting a short limited debate just to keep the Liberal government from doing the country's business. Last Thursday (Hansard, page 7343) he promptly supported Mr. Knowles' urging that the government devote two days a week to other business while the flag debate lasts. Mr. Favreau, for Mr. Pearson, would not accept this.
Mr. Diefenbaker refuses to limit debate for it is the one weapon that might oblige Mr. Pearson to produce a more acceptable flag. (We've met mighty few people of any political persuasion who really like the present suggestion.)
If Mr. Pearson came forward with a design more adequately representing the nation's wishes the opposition would vote it through to happy fulfilment in weeks, not months.
The obstacle to peaceful solution is the present design, not the debate schedule.
Whatever flag parliament eventually passes should be honoured by us all. The country's impatience is not for any new flag but a new flag it wants. Reasonable debate and the devotion of compromise can produce such a flag.
We've had enough of Liberals saying Tories are anti-French, and Tories saying Liberals are selling out to the French.
Let's go on with the business of the country, and finding an acceptable flag, at one and the same time-for the two can't be separated now.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it 10.30?
